title: Iraqi Oil Tanker VLCC Agios Fanourios I Resumes Voyage to Vietnam After US Navy Hold in Gulf of Oman
summary: The Maltese-flagged VLCC Agios Fanourios I resumed its voyage toward Vietnam on May 16 after the U.S. Navy held the supertanker for five days in the Gulf of Oman as part of its ongoing blockade enforcement against Iran. The vessel carries Iraqi crude oil destined for Vietnam's Nghi Son refinery.
contents:
## Iraqi Crude Supertanker Released After US Navy Detention

### Vessel Movement Details

The Maltese-flagged Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) Agios Fanourios I departed the Strait of Hormuz on May 10 and sailed into the Gulf of Oman before executing a U-turn on May 11. The supertanker remained under U.S. Navy detention for five days before receiving approval to continue its voyage on May 16. Athens-based vessel manager Eastern Mediterranean Maritime confirmed the tanker now heads toward Vietnam's Nghi Son refinery, with an expected arrival date of May 30.

### Blockade Context

U.S. Central Command confirmed the vessel redirection as part of ongoing enforcement of the naval blockade against Iran, which began on April 13. The tanker carried Iraqi crude oil — not Iranian cargo — yet fell under broader scrutiny as all traffic through the strait faces heightened inspection protocols. A VLCC can carry up to two million barrels of oil, making each transit through the chokepoint a significant logistical and strategic calculation.

### Shipping Confidence Remains Fragile

Ship broker Clarksons noted that shipping confidence around the Strait of Hormuz remains "very weak." Only 12 ships crossed the strait in the prior 24 hours, including two liquefied petroleum gas tankers bound for India. Before the conflict, the strait served as the conduit for 20% of the world's energy supplies, equating to 125 to 140 daily vessel passages. The dramatic reduction in traffic volume underscores the continuing disruption to global energy supply chains.

title: Russian LNG Export Revenue Declines as Shift to Asian Markets Doubles Logistics Costs
summary: Russia faces declining liquefied natural gas export revenue as the pivot from European to Asian buyers at least doubles transport costs. Industry sources reported that India refused to purchase a cargo from Russia's U.S.-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 plant due to expense and sanctions complications.
contents:
## Russian LNG Revenue Takes Hit from Asian Market Pivot

### European Market Loss Forces Costly Rerouting

Russia's diversification of LNG exports to Asia following the loss of European market access will significantly cut revenue due to at least a doubling of logistics costs, according to industry sources and analysts. The European Union plans to fully phase out Russian LNG imports by early 2027 as part of its sanctions pressure over the Ukraine conflict. President Vladimir Putin stated in early March that Russia could halt gas supplies to Europe immediately and seek longer-term commitments from other buyers.

### India Refuses Sanctioned Cargo

The challenges confronting Moscow became apparent when India refused to purchase a cargo from Russia's U.S.-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 plant. One industry source explained that Russian LNG proved too expensive once transport costs and sanctions-related complications factored in. A trip from the Yamal LNG plant on Russia's Arctic peninsula to Europe takes approximately 17 to 20 days, compared with 50 to 60 days via the Suez Canal to Asia, 70 to 80 days via the Cape of Good Hope, or 50 to 65 days via the Northern Sea Route.

### Transport Cost Analysis

Transport costs from Yamal to a European port average $1 to $1.5 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), while costs to India reach $2.5 to $5 per mmBtu. The Northern Sea Route represents the most expensive option for South Asian deliveries due to the shortage of ice-class tankers. The cheapest Asia-bound route runs via the Suez Canal with transshipment in Murmansk, costing $2.6 to $2.7 per mmBtu. These economics fundamentally challenge Russia's energy export strategy and diminish revenue projections for its Arctic gas infrastructure.

title: Berg Propulsion Contracted to Supply Propulsion Systems for Four Powerful Diesel-Electric Tugs Built in Turkiye
summary: Berg Propulsion secured a contract to supply propulsion and control systems for four diesel-electric firefighting offshore support tugs ordered by Smit Lamnalco from Uzmar Shipyard in Turkiye. The vessels will feature bollard pull capacities exceeding 130 tons, making them the most powerful tugs of their type ever constructed in the country.
contents:
## Berg Propulsion Wins Contract for Record-Breaking Turkish Tugs

### Contract Details

Berg Propulsion received a contract to supply propulsion and control systems for four diesel-electric firefighting offshore support tugs. Smit Lamnalco ordered the vessels from builder Uzmar Shipyard, with initial deployment planned for French Guyana. Berg expects to deliver equipment for the first vessel in November 2026, with the final delivery scheduled by July 2027.

### Technical Specifications

Built to Canadian naval architect Robert Allan Limited's RAmpage 6000-DE design, each 60-meter tug will feature twin 4,000kW electric motors. Berg's propulsive package includes two MTA836 Z drive fixed-pitch azimuth thrusters, two MTT216 controllable-pitch bow thrusters, and an MPC800 control system. The vessels will carry bollard pull capacities exceeding 130 tons, representing a significant step up from the largest tugs Uzmar has built to date.

### Strategic Significance

The Bureau Veritas-classed vessels consolidate Berg's presence in Turkiye, which has emerged as a major construction hub for tug innovation. The order demonstrates continued demand for high-capacity offshore support vessels capable of performing firefighting and towing operations in demanding maritime environments. The diesel-electric configuration provides operational flexibility and fuel efficiency advantages compared to conventional propulsion arrangements, reflecting broader industry trends toward electrification of marine propulsion systems.

title: USNI Fleet Tracker Reports Two Carrier Strike Groups Operating in Arabian Sea Supporting Iran Blockade
summary: The USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker for May 18, 2026 reports the Abraham Lincoln and George H.W. Bush Carrier Strike Groups operating in the Arabian Sea in support of Operation Epic Fury, while the USS Gerald R. Ford returned to Norfolk after a historic 326-day deployment.
contents:
## U.S. Navy Fleet Deployment Update — May 18, 2026

### Arabian Sea Operations
The Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CVN-72) and the George H.W. Bush Carrier Strike Group (CVN-77) continue operating in the Arabian Sea, enforcing the naval blockade against Iran under Operation Epic Fury. Carrier Air Wing 9 embarked aboard Lincoln, while Carrier Air Wing 7 deployed with Bush. Combined, these strike groups field more than 150 combat aircraft and nine guided-missile destroyers loaded with offensive and defensive missile systems.

### USS Gerald R. Ford Returns Home
Aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78) completed a record-breaking 326-day combat deployment and returned to Naval Station Norfolk on May 16, 2026. Ford deployed across U.S. European Command, U.S. Southern Command, and U.S. Central Command areas of responsibility, supporting Operation Absolute Resolve in the Caribbean and Operation Epic Fury in the Middle East. The crew received the Presidential Unit Citation upon arrival.

### Indo-Pacific Movements
USS George Washington (CVN-73) returned to Yokosuka, Japan, after completing a shakedown cruise following a brief pierside availability. The Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, including USS Boxer (LHD-4), USS Comstock (LSD-45), and USS Portland (LPD-27), operates in the Strait of Malacca with the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit.

### Caribbean and Mediterranean
The Iwo Jima Amphibious Ready Group, including USS Fort Lauderdale (LPD-28), operates in the Caribbean Sea with the 22nd Marine Expeditionary Unit. In the Eastern Mediterranean, independently deployed guided-missile destroyers USS Bulkeley (DDG-84), USS Gonzalez (DDG-66), USS Arleigh Burke (DDG-51), and USS Oscar Austin (DDG-79) maintain presence.

### Red Sea
USS Thomas Hudner (DDG-116) operates in the Red Sea, maintaining situational awareness and regional security posture.

### Force Posture Summary
The U.S. Navy maintains 291 total battle force ships, with 101 deployed (70 USS, 31 USNS) and 85 underway. This deployment tempo reflects the heightened operational demands of the Iran conflict and ongoing global maritime security commitments.

title: Philippines and China Exchange Fresh Accusations Over Second Thomas Shoal Resupply Mission
summary: The Philippine Coast Guard reported harassment and dangerous maneuvers from Chinese ships during a resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal, while Beijing accused Manila of transporting construction materials to reinforce the grounded BRP Sierra Madre.
contents:
## Philippines-China Confrontation at Second Thomas Shoal

### Resupply Mission Under Pressure
Philippine vessels attempted to deliver supplies to troops stationed aboard the grounded BRP Sierra Madre at Second Thomas Shoal (Ayungin Shoal) on May 18, 2026. Chinese coast guard and maritime militia ships moved to monitor and challenge the operation, according to statements from both governments.

### Philippine Response
The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea condemned what it described as "illegal, aggressive and destabilizing" actions by the China Coast Guard (CCG) and Chinese maritime militia vessels inside the Philippines' Exclusive Economic Zone. The Philippine Coast Guard reported that escort vessels encountered harassment and dangerous maneuvers from Chinese ships during the mission.

### Mission Outcome
Despite the confrontation, Philippine officials confirmed the mission succeeded and supplies reached troops stationed aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, a World War II-era ship intentionally grounded on the shoal in 1999 to reinforce Manila's territorial claim. The shoal lies roughly 200 kilometers from the Philippine island of Palawan and falls within the Philippines' internationally recognized EEZ under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

### Beijing's Counter-Narrative
China rejected Manila's account and insisted its coast guard acted lawfully in waters Beijing considers under Chinese jurisdiction. A China Coast Guard spokesperson said Chinese vessels issued warnings, monitored the Philippine boats, and "regulated" their movements. Beijing also accused the Philippines of transporting construction materials to reinforce what it called an "illegally grounded warship."

### Broader Context
This latest confrontation comes amid a broader increase in maritime tensions across the region. Earlier this month, the Philippine Coast Guard accused China of conducting illegal marine scientific research near Pag-asa Island, where Chinese personnel from the Xiang Yang Hong 33 research vessel landed on two sandbars within Philippine territorial waters. The Philippines has expanded military cooperation with the United States, Australia, Japan, and other allies through joint military exercises, including the recently concluded Balikatan 2026.
